rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic alphabet names are conventionally pronounced as cut two-letter forms with imala or three-letter forms with an open, lengthened middle alif; zay permits either treatment depending on whether its y is voiced.
rows.anchor: أن حروف المعجم على نوعين ثنائي وثلاثي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Full fath is the underlying rule and imala is derivative, so every imala can be opened but not every open vowel can be imala-ed.
rows.anchor: إشباع الفتحة في جميع المواضع أصل والإمالة فرع عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers use three approaches: open both vowels, imala both, or combine the underlying and derivative treatments by opening one and inclining the other.
rows.anchor: للقراء في القراءات المخصوصة بهذا الموضع ثلاثة طرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One rationale for combining the two treatments is to honor both the basic full vowel and the widely used derivative imala.
rows.anchor: الفتحة المشبعة أصل والإمالة فرع مشهور كثير الاستعمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another rationale is that the letters are separated in speech but joined in writing, so the reading honors both spoken separation and written connection.
rows.anchor: مقطوعان في اللفظ موصولان في الخط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The familiar reading opens both hāʾ and yāʾ.
rows.anchor: القراءة المعروفة فيه فتحة الهاء والياء جميعا

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن مبادر والقطعي عن أيوب
rows.claim: They incline hāʾ and open yāʾ, distinguishing it from the demonstrative hāʾ, which is never inclined.
rows.anchor: كسر الهاء وفتح الياء وهي قراءة أبي عمرو وابن مبادر

rows.speaker: حمزة والأعمش وطلحة والضحاك عن عاصم
rows.claim: They open hāʾ and incline yāʾ because yāʾ is the sister of kasra, making kasra more fitting there.
rows.anchor: فتح الهاء وكسر الياء وهو قراءة حمزة والأعمش وطلحة

rows.speaker: الكسائي والمفضل ويحيى عن عاصم والوليد بن أسلم عن ابن عامر والزهري وابن جرير
rows.claim: They incline both hāʾ and yāʾ for the previously given reasons.
rows.anchor: إمالتهما جميعا وهي قراءة الكسائي والمفضل ويحيى عن عاصم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan is reported to read one of hāʾ and yāʾ with ḍamma and the other open; al-Kashshāf also transmits both with ḍamma.
rows.anchor: قراءة الحسن وهي ضم الهاء وفتح الياء ، وعنه أيضا فتح الهاء وضم الياء

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinnī records Hasan's reading as ḍamma on one letter and fath on the other, without fixing which one.
rows.anchor: لأنه أورد ابن جنى في كتاب ( المكتسب ) أن قراءة الحسن ضم أحدهما وفتح الآخر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A rationale for Hasan's ḍamma is that he imagined each letter's middle alif derived from wāw, whose preceding vowel is ḍamma.
rows.anchor: تصور أن عين الفعل في الهاء والياء ألف منقلب عن الواو

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: A further transmitted reading applies a trace of ḍamma to both letters.
rows.anchor: وسادسها : ها يا بإشمامهما شيئا من الضمة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar separates the letters with brief pauses and pronounces the nūn of ʿayn clearly; other readers join the letters and conceal the nūn.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر كهيعص يفصل الحروف بعضها من بعض بأدنى سكتة

rows.speaker: عاصم ويعقوب
rows.claim: They pronounce the ṣād clearly, whereas the familiar reading assimilates it.
rows.anchor: القراءة المعروفة صاد ، ذكر بالإدغام ، وعن عاصم ويعقوب بالإظهار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads the letters as God's praise of Himself: Kāf means sufficient, hāʾ guide, ʿayn knowing, and ṣād truthful.
rows.anchor: أن قوله تعالى كهيعص ثناء من الله على نفسه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also interprets kāf as the Mighty or Generous, yāʾ as Generous or Wise, and ʿayn as Mighty or Just; al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas says yāʾ means Protector.
rows.anchor: أنه حمل الكاف على الكبير والكريم ، ويحكى أيضا عنه أنه حمل الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī rejects these coded expansions because Arabic supplies no evidence for them; choosing one possible divine name over others would be arbitrary and license unsupported esoteric readings.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز من الله تعالى أن يودع كتابه ما لا تدل عليه اللغة لا بالحقيقة ولا بالمجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr has four readings: verbal noun, past tense with gemination, past tense without gemination, and imperative.
rows.anchor: في لفظة ذكر أربع قراءات صيغة المصدر أو الماضي مخففة أو مشددة أو الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the verbal noun, raḥmata is genitive and three case patterns follow: both ʿabda and Zakariyyāʾ accusative; both nominative in Ibn ʿĀmir; or the first accusative and the second nominative.
rows.anchor: أما صيغة المصدر فلا بد فيها من كسر رحمة ربك على الإضافة

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir raises both ʿabd and Zakariyyāʾ, making them appositional explanations of the mercy.
rows.anchor: برفعهما والمعنى وتلك الرحمة هي عبده زكرياء عن ابن عامر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The geminated past-tense reading requires raḥmata in the accusative.
rows.anchor: وأما صيغة الماضي بالتشديد فلا بد فيها من نصب رحمة

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: For the ungeminated past, al-Kalbī reads rabbuka nominative with the sense that the Lord mentioned His servant Zakariyyā, or places rabbaka accusative before a nominative ʿabdu Zakariyyā.
rows.anchor: وهاتان القراءتان للكلبي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase as an imperative, with raḥmata accusative.
rows.anchor: وهي قراءة ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On either the verbal-noun or past-tense parsing, the implied subject is this recited passage: a mention of the Lord's mercy.
rows.anchor: هذا المتلو من القرآن ذكر رحمة ربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation identifies the mercy with Zakariyyā himself, who was a mercy to his people by guiding them to faith and obedience.
rows.anchor: أن يكون رحمة على أمته لأنه هداهم إلى الإيمان والطاعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation makes Zakariyyā a mercy to Muhammad and his community because his sincerity and appeal to God model a path for them.
rows.anchor: يكون رحمة على نبينا محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم وعلى أمة محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase means that this sūrah recounts the mercy God showed His servant Zakariyyā.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة فيها ذكر الرحمة التي رحم بها عبدة زكرياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakariyyā hid his call in keeping with God's practice: secrecy avoids show and better expresses sincerity, although loud and quiet calls are equal before God.
rows.anchor: لأن الجهر والإخفاء عند الله سيان فكان الإخفاء أولى لأنه أبعد عن الرياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says he concealed the request lest people blame him for seeking a child in old age.
rows.anchor: أخفاه لئلا يلام على طلب الولد في زمان الشيخوخة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says he kept it from the relatives whose conduct he feared.
rows.anchor: أسره من مواليه الذين خافهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation attributes the quiet voice to his weakness and advanced age.
rows.anchor: خفي صوته لضعفه وهرمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call can be both a nidāʾ and quiet: he raised his voice as much as he could, but age made it faint, so intention made it a call and reality made it quiet.
rows.anchor: فكان نداء نظرا إلى قصده وخفيا نظرا إلى الواقع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, he prayed during the ritual prayer, since the angels answered while he stood praying in the sanctuary; supplication in prayer would be quiet.
rows.anchor: فنادته الملئكة وهو قائم يصلى فى المحراب

rows.speaker: القراء
rows.claim: The word wahn is read with each of the three vowel patterns.
rows.anchor: قرىء { وهن } بالحركات الثلاث

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr assimilates sīn into shīn in min al-raʾsi shayban.
rows.anchor: إدغام السين في الشين ( من الرأس شيبا ) عن أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī is reported to give the yāʾ of al-mawālī sukūn in the reading with fatḥa on the yāʾ of innī khiftu.
rows.anchor: بفتح الياء وعن الزهري بإسكان الياء من الموالي

rows.speaker: عثمان وعلي بن الحسين ومحمد بن علي وسعيد بن جبير وزيد بن ثابت وابن عباس
rows.claim: They read khiftu with doubled, open khāʾ and fāʾ and kasra on tāʾ; warāʾī then means after me, as the successors have dwindled and need support to uphold religion.
rows.anchor: قرأ عثمان وعلي بن الحسين ومحمد بن علي وسعيد بن جبير وزيد بن ثابت وابن عباس خفت

rows.speaker: عثمان وعلي بن الحسين ومحمد بن علي وسعيد بن جبير وزيد بن ثابت وابن عباس
rows.claim: With the same reading, warāʾī may mean before me: the relatives have passed on, leaving no support or strength.
rows.anchor: أن يكون بمعنى قدامي والمعنى أنهم خفوا قدامه ودرجوا

rows.speaker: حميد بن مقسم
rows.claim: Ḥumayd ibn Miqsam reads min warāʾī with a fatḥa on the yāʾ; Ibn Kathīr instead reads warāya as in ʿaṣāya.
rows.anchor: وعن حميد بن مقسم كذلك لكن بفتح الياء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو والكسائي والزهري والأعمش وطلحة
rows.claim: They read both yarithni and yarith with jazm as responses to the supplication, unlike the familiar nominative reading that makes them adjectives.
rows.anchor: القراءة المعروفة بالرفع فيهما صفة

rows.speaker: علي ابن أبي طالب وابن عباس وجعفر بن محمد والحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: They read waliyyan yarithni with yarithni as an active participle in the jussive form, wāriṯ.
rows.anchor: عن علي ابن أبي طالب وابن عباس وجعفر بن محمد والحسن وقتادة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported to read yarithni as wāriṯ from the family of Jacob.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس : { يرثنى } وارث من آل يعقوب

rows.speaker: الجحدري
rows.claim: Al-Jaḥdarī reads yarith in a diminutive active-participle form, ufayʿil.
rows.anchor: عن الجحدري { ويرث } تصغير وارث على وزن أفيعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wahn means weakness; the Kashshāf likens gray hair to a flame in whiteness, brightness, spread through the hair, and taking hold, then analyzes the phrase as a metaphor with shayban as specification.
rows.anchor: الوهن ضعف القوة قال في ( الكشاف ) شبه الشيب بشواظ النار في بياضه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The metaphor makes the head, the hair's source, the subject of the spreading, and leaves its identity as Zakariyyā's head understood rather than stated.
rows.anchor: أسند الاشتعال إلى مكان الشعر ومنبته وهو الرأس وأخرج الشيب مميزا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Duʿāʾ means requesting an act, with response as its opposite; the act can be attributed either to its agent or to its object.
rows.anchor: وأما الدعاء فطلب الفعل ومقابله الإجابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root w-l-y conveys nearness: the poem by Saʿida ibn Juʾba uses it for being near; derivatives include a following rain, saddlecloth, guardian, and ruler because each is close to what it concerns.
rows.anchor: وكل مما يليك وجلست مما ايليه ومنه الولي وهو المطر الذي يلي الوسمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waliya ʿannī, to turn away, uses an intensified infix with privative force; awlā, more deserving, also implies greater nearness to the thing.
rows.anchor: أما ولي عني إذا أدبر فهو من باب تثقيل الحشو للسلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawlā names the place or relation of being close, as marma and mabnā name the place of throwing and building.
rows.anchor: والمولى اسم لموضع الولي كالمرمى والمبني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿĀqir means a woman who does not bear children; the word derives from wound or maiming, as barrenness is a defect in the original constitution.
rows.anchor: وأما العاقر فهي التي لا تلد والعقر في اللغة الجرح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āl are a person's close associates whose affairs return to him, whether kin, companions as in Pharaoh's family, or those sharing a faith as the Prophet's family.
rows.anchor: فهم خاصة الرجل الذين يؤول أمرهم إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakariyyā presents three grounds before his request: his weakness, God's record of never rejecting his prayer, and the religious benefit of what he seeks.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن زكرياء عليه السلام قدم على السؤال أمورا ثلاثة : أحدها : كونه ضعيفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He first describes inner weakness: bones are the body's hardest members, supporting the other organs and protecting them, so if they weaken the softer organs must be weaker still.
rows.anchor: العظام أصلب الأعضاء التي في البدن وجعلت كذلك لمنفعتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because bones carry the other organs, their weakness entails weakness in what they carry; gray hair then displays the weakness outwardly, making the appeal emphasize reliance on God's power over visible causes.
rows.anchor: تطرق الضعف إلى الحامل موجبا لتطرقه إلى المحمول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bones also serve as shields for vulnerable parts such as the skull and chest, so their structural strength is essential.
rows.anchor: لأن تكون جنة يقوى بها ما سواها من الأعضاء بمنزلة قحف الرأس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakariyyā appeals to God's earlier acceptance in two ways: rejecting him now would undermine the earlier favor, and denying a habitual response after years of acceptance would be especially painful.
rows.anchor: إنك ما رددتني في أول الأمر مع أني ما تعودت لطفك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A refusal is even more painful from a benefactor, especially when the supplicant is now physically and emotionally weaker than before.
rows.anchor: بعد ما عودتني القبول مع نهاية ضعفي لكان ذلك بالغا إلى الغاية القصوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic says a person is saʿīd in a need when he obtains it and shaqī when he misses it; bi-duʿāʾika means my calling upon You, with the act attached to its object.
rows.anchor: تقول سعد فلان بحاجته إذا ظفر بها وشقي بها إذا خاب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: They understand al-mawālī as heirs who would follow Zakariyyā.
rows.anchor: الأول : قال ابن عباس والحسن : إني خفت الموالي أي الورثة من بعدي

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets al-mawālī as the agnatic relatives.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد العصبة

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abū Ṣāliḥ interprets al-mawālī as the kalāla, relatives outside direct descendants and ascendants.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي صالح الكلالة

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Aṣamm identifies them as paternal cousins, those next to him in lineage.
rows.anchor: وعن الأصم بنو العم وهم الذين يلونه في النسب

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim allows mawlā to mean ally, cousin, owner, or companion; here it is whoever would take his place in inheritance.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي مسلم المولي يراد به الناصر وابن العم والمالك والصاحب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mawālī are those succeeding him in political authority, wealth, or care of religious affairs; those nearest to a religious authority customarily have an assigned role during his life.
rows.anchor: والمختار أن المراد من الموالي الذين يخلفون بعده إما في السياسة أو في المال

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One view says Zakariyyā feared that his heirs would corrupt the religion.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم : خافهم على إفساد الدين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view says he feared their taking over his property or other affairs after his death despite lacking the knowledge and ability for the role.
rows.anchor: خاف أن ينتهي أمره إليهم بعد موته في مال وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third possibility is that God told him only one Israelite prophet with a father remained, so he feared his cousin would be the next prophet and asked for a son to fill that role.
rows.anchor: لم يبق من أنبياء بني إسرائيل نبي له أب إلا واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakariyyā may have held prophetic, political, and priestly leadership and feared the successors in one or all of those roles.
rows.anchor: كان إليه مع النبوة السياسة من جهة الملك وما يتصل بالإمامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although khift is past tense, it describes continuing fear, as in ordinary speech saying I have feared that something may happen; kānat imraʾatī ʿāqiran likewise describes her current barrenness and emphasizes its long duration.
rows.anchor: خرج على لفظ الماضي لكنه يفيد أنه في المستقبل أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using the past for barrenness stresses how long it has lasted and strengthens the point that conception is ordinarily unlikely; Arabic also sometimes substitutes past for future and vice versa.
rows.anchor: في الإخبار عنه بلفظ الماضي إعلام بتقادم العهد في ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda takes min warāʾī to mean before me, while others take it as after my death; both senses are possible.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة أي قدامي وبين يدي وقال آخرون أي بعد موتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One can fear future heirs based on signs and reasonable expectation, such as their apparent persistence in corrupt behavior.
rows.anchor: إن ذلك قد يعرف بالأمارات والظن وذلك كاف في حصول الخوف

rows.speaker: الأكثرون
rows.claim: Most interpreters say waliyyan means a child.
rows.anchor: فالأكثرون على أنه طلب الولد

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others say Zakariyyā asked for someone to take his place, whether or not that person was his child.
rows.anchor: طلب من يقوم مقامه ولدا كان أو غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He most likely asked for a child: the request for good offspring in 3:38, the inheritance request here, and the plea not to be left alone in 21:89 together make that reading clearest.
rows.anchor: والأقرب هو الأول لثلاثة أوجه

rows.speaker: أصحاب القول الثالث
rows.claim: Those who say he did not seek a particular child argue that his astonishment at the later announcement would be odd if he had prayed specifically for a child.
rows.anchor: احتج أصحاب القول الثالث بأنه لما بشر بالولد استعظم على سبيل التعجب

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says Zakariyyā asked whether a child would be granted while he and his wife remained as they were or after both became young again.
rows.anchor: وهذا يحكي عن الحسن

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another explanation says he asked for a child either from his wife if God made her fertile or from another woman; after the glad tidings he asked which, and learned it would be from his wife.
rows.anchor: إني أيست أن يكون لي منها ولد فهب لي من لدنك وليا كيف شئت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن والضحاك
rows.claim: They interpret both instances of inheritance as inheritance of property.
rows.anchor: أن المراد بالميراث في الموضعين هو وراثة المال وهذا قول ابن عباس والحسن والضحاك

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abū Ṣāliḥ interprets both inheritances as prophethood.
rows.anchor: أن المراد به في الموضعين وراثة النبوة وهو قول أبي صالح

rows.speaker: السدي ومجاهد والشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī, Mujāhid, and al-Shaʿbī say he inherits Zakariyyā's property and the prophethood of Jacob's family; this is also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.
rows.anchor: يرثني المال ويرث من آل يعقوب النبوة وهو قول السدي ومجاهد والشعبي

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid is also reported to say that he inherits knowledge from Zakariyyā and prophethood from Jacob's family.
rows.anchor: يرثني العلم ويرث من آل يعقوب النبوة وهو مروي عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reported meanings reduce to property, priestly office, knowledge, prophethood, or a righteous way of life; inheritance language can cover each.
rows.anchor: ترجع إلى أحد أمور خمسة وهي المال ومنصب الحبورة والعلم والنبوة والسيرة الحسنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic usage calls land, homes, and property inherited, and also says that Moses' guidance and scripture were bequeathed to Israel.
rows.anchor: وأورثكم أرضهم وديارهم وأمولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's report that scholars are heirs of prophets supports inheritance of knowledge; the cited passage about David and Solomon can signify either kingship or prophethood.
rows.anchor: العلماء ورثة الأنبياء ، وإن الأنبياء لم يورثوا دينارا ولا درهما

rows.speaker: أصحاب وراثة المال
rows.claim: Those favoring property cite a report asking God to have mercy on Zakariyyā because he had no heir, taking it as evidence of property inheritance.
rows.anchor: رحم الله زكريا ما كان له من يرثه

rows.speaker: أصحاب وراثة المال
rows.claim: Their rational argument is that knowledge, exemplary conduct, and prophethood are acquired rather than inherited, so the term should mean property.
rows.anchor: العلم والسيرة والنبوة لا تورث بل لا تحصل إلا بالاكتساب

rows.speaker: أصحاب وراثة المال
rows.claim: They argue that asking God to make the heir pleasing would be unnecessary if prophethood were intended, since a prophet must already be pleasing and protected from sin.
rows.anchor: لو كان المراد من الإرث إرث النبوة لكان قد سأل جعل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم رضيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophetic statement that prophets leave no inheritance does not rule out this request if the report is specific to Zakariyyā.
rows.anchor: فهذا لا يمنع أن يكون خاصا به

rows.speaker: أصحاب وراثة العلم والنبوة
rows.claim: Those who understand inheritance as religious office say prophets care less about property, though Zakariyyā may have possessed wealth useful to religion.
rows.anchor: اهتمامهم لا يشتد بأمر المال كما يشتد بأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic inheritance can mean a child taking the father's place and continuing his religious work, just as property inheritance lets an heir manage what belonged to the father.
rows.anchor: فكذلك إذا كان المعلوم في الإبن أن يصير نبيا بعده فيقوم بأمر الدين بعده جاز أن يقال ورثه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although a plural no-inheritance report might be metaphorically applied to one person, its literal plural and variant wording favor the general sense; inheritance should cover everything that perpetuates religious benefit, including knowledge, conduct, office, prophethood, and useful property.
rows.anchor: والأولى أن يحمل ذلك على كل ما فيه نفع وصلاح في الدين

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most interpreters identify Jacob as Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham; the genealogies cited explain how Zakariyyā and his wife connect to the tribes of Israel.
rows.anchor: اتفق أكثر المفسرين على أن يعقوب ههنا هو يعقوب بن إسحاق بن إبراهيم

rows.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and Muqātil instead identify Jacob as son of Mattān and brother of ʿImrān, with Jacob's family being Yaḥyā's maternal uncles.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المفسرين ليس المراد من يعقوب ههنا ولد إسحاق بن إبراهيم

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the Mattān family led Israel and that Zakariyyā, head of the priests, wanted his son to inherit priestly office and their kingship.
rows.anchor: كان بنو ماثان رؤوس بني إسرائيل وملوكهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading of pleasing is that Yaḥyā would excel even among the prophets, fulfilled by his being a master, chaste, prophet, righteous, and free of sin or intent to sin.
rows.anchor: المراد واجعله رضيا من الأنبياء وذلك لأن كلهم مرضيون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading is that his community would accept him and not meet him with denial.
rows.anchor: أن يكون رضيا في أمته لا يتلقى بالتكذيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading is that no accusation or fault could be attached to him.
rows.anchor: أن لا يكون متهما في شيء ولا يوجد فيه مطعن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth compares the request to Abraham and Ishmael's plea to be made submissive despite already being so: it asks either for steadfastness or a superior rank among submitters.
rows.anchor: وكانا في ذلك الوقت مسلمين ، وكأن المراد هناك ثبتنا على هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is evidence that God creates human acts: Zakariyyā asks God to make Yaḥyā pleasing, which concerns his action.
rows.anchor: لأنه إنما يكون رضيا بفعله ، فلما سأل الله تعالى جعله رضيا

rows.speaker: أصحاب الألطاف
rows.claim: An objection says God makes him pleasing by granting graces after which he freely chooses approval.
rows.anchor: المراد منه أن يلطف له بضروب الألطاف فيختار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī rejects that response because making him pleasing through enabling graces is a nonliteral reading, and a grace obligatory on God could not properly be requested in prayer.
rows.anchor: لكان ذلك مجازا وهو خلاف الأصل

rows.speaker: الأكثرون
rows.claim: Most interpreters say God is the one calling to Zakariyyā, because the surrounding speech before and after is his address to God.
rows.anchor: فالأكثرون على أنه هو الله تعالى وذلك لأن ما قبل هذه الآية يدل

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others say an angel calls, citing the explicit account that the angels called while Zakariyyā prayed and the subsequent wording your Lord has said.
rows.anchor: فنادته الملئكة وهو قائم يصلى فى المحراب أن الله يبشرك بيحيى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angel interpretation can be reconciled with the first view if both God and angels announced the glad tidings.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يقال حصل النداءان نداء الله ونداء الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase your Lord has said in the next verse can itself be spoken by God, so it does not require an angel as speaker.
rows.anchor: يمكن أن يكون كلام الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent problem of either seeking a child without permission or receiving a redundant announcement has two answers: a personal request may be made without permission, or permission may have been given while its timing remained unknown.
rows.anchor: فيجوز أن يسأل بغير إذن ، ويحتمل أنه أذن له فيه ولم يعلم وقته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وسعيد بن جبير وعكرمة وقتادة
rows.claim: They understand sami as a namesake: no one had previously been given the name Yaḥyā.
rows.anchor: وهو قول ابن عباس والحسن وسعيد بن جبير وعكرمة وقتادة أنه لم يسم أحد قبله بهذا الاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes sami as an equal or counterpart, as in the later question whether one knows any equal to God.
rows.anchor: أن المراد بالسمي النظير كما في قوله : { هل تعلم له سميا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One proposed counterpart is a prophet matching Yaḥyā in being masterly, chaste, and free from sin, echoing the request that God make him pleasing.
rows.anchor: أنه سيد وحصور لم يعص ولم يهم بمعصية كأنه جواب لقوله : { واجعله رب رضيا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī calls this weak because it would place Yaḥyā above earlier prophets such as Adam, Noah, Abraham, and Moses, contrary to consensus.
rows.anchor: وهذا الوجه ضعيف لأنه يقتضي تفضيله على الأنبياء الذين كانوا قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further reading says God uniquely named Yaḥyā before he existed, whereas people normally receive names only after birth.
rows.anchor: فإن الله تعالى هو الذي سماه قبل دخوله في الوجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation makes his unusual birth to an old man and infertile woman the unprecedented feature.
rows.anchor: أنه ولد بين شيخ فان وعجوز عاقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī prefers the literal namesake meaning because counterpart is a nonliteral shift without need; the context of worship in 19:65 requires that shift there, but not here, and a unique royal name honors its bearer.
rows.anchor: الوجه الأول أولى وذلك لأن حمل السمي على النظير وإن كان يفيد المدح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās that Yaḥyā's name means God restored his mother's barrenness to fertility.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أن الله تعالى أحيا به عقر أمه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says God made Yaḥyā's heart alive through faith and obedience, linking spiritual life to 6:122 and 8:24.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة أن الله تعالى أحيا قلبه بالإيمان والطاعة

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says everyone has sinned or intended to sin except Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā, who neither intended nor committed sin.
rows.anchor: ما من أحد إلا وقد عصى أو هم إلا يحيى بن زكريا

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم بن حبيب
rows.claim: Abū al-Qāsim ibn Ḥabīb says Yaḥyā was named for martyrdom, since martyrs are alive with their Lord.
rows.anchor: عن أبي القاسم بن حبيب أنه استشهد وأن الشهداء أحياء عند ربهم

rows.speaker: عمرو بن عبد الله المقدسي
rows.claim: ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Maqdisī tells a naming story in which God calls Sarah to give a letter of her name to the servant Ḥayy, yielding Yaḥyā.
rows.anchor: أوحى الله تعالى إلى إبراهيم عليه السلام أن قل ليسارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says Yaḥyā first believed in Jesus: while their mothers were pregnant, the unborn Yaḥyā bowed to Jesus in Mary's womb.
rows.anchor: أن يحيى عليه السلام أول من آمن بعيسى فصار قلبه حيا بذلك الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A final explanation says religion itself comes alive through Yaḥyā, since Zakariyyā asked for him for religion's sake.
rows.anchor: أن الدين يحيا به لأنه إنما سأله زكريا لأجل الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī judges these etymologies weak: proper names need not derive a descriptive meaning, but function as identifying signs.
rows.anchor: هذه الوجوه ضعيفة لأن أسماء الألقاب لا يطلب فيها وجه الاشتقاق

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read ʿitiyyan, ṣiliyyan, jithiyyan, and bukiyyan with kasra; Ḥafṣ has ḍamma for bukiyyan and kasra for the rest, while other readers use ḍamma throughout.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي عتيا وصليا وجثيا وبكيا بكسر العين والصاد والجيم والباء

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads ʿitiyyan and ṣiliyyan with fatḥa on the initial consonants.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود بفتح العين والصاد من عتيا وصليا

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب وابن عباس
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn ʿAbbās read ʿasiyyan with sīn rather than ṭāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي بن كعب وابن عباس عسيا بالسين غير المعجمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghulām first means a male at the onset of sexual desire, from ightalama, then extends to a young pupil such as Thʿalab's student.
rows.anchor: الغلام الإنسان الذكر في ابتداء شهوته للجماع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿItī and ʿasī are variants for a person changed by age into hardship; ʿāsī describes this condition, and ʿāt can describe a long or very dark night.
rows.anchor: العتي والعبسي واحد تقول عتا يعتو عتوا وعتيا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl explains that ʿāqir has no feminine tāʾ because some feminine adjectives on the fāʿil pattern have no corresponding masculine form; the same pattern can describe a masculine noun as feminine.
rows.anchor: قال الخليل : هذه الصفات مذكرة وصف بها المؤنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first question is why Zakariyyā asked how he could have a son after requesting one; the second is whether his surprise implied doubt in God's power, which would be improper for a prophet.
rows.anchor: لم تعجب بقوله : { أنى يكون لي غلام } مع أنه هو الذي طلب الغلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If he had not sought a particular child, the first problem disappears; otherwise, how can ask whether God would restore youth to him and his wife or grant a child despite their age, as an inquiry rather than disbelief.
rows.anchor: هو التعجب من أنه تعالى يجعلهما شابين ثم يرزقهما الولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The restoration interpretation is supported by 21:89-90, where God answers by restoring his wife's capacity to bear.
rows.anchor: وما هذا الإصلاح إلا أنه أعاد قوة الولادة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says Satan told Zakariyyā the announcement was a mockery rather than God's word, so Zakariyyā asked how he could have a boy.
rows.anchor: ذكر السدي في الجواب وجها آخر فقال : إنه لما سمع النداء بالبشارة

rows.speaker: بعض المتكلمين
rows.claim: Some theologians reject al-Suddī's account because if prophets could suspect revelation came from Satan, confidence in revelation would collapse.
rows.anchor: هذا باطل قطعا إذ لو جوز الأنبياء في بعض ما يرد عن الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A possible reply is that uncertainty may occur at first and disappear through a confirming miracle, which may have been absent in this instance.
rows.anchor: هذا الاحتمال قائم في أول الأمر وإنما يزول بالمعجزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The announcement does not explicitly say the child is his; Zakariyyā may tactfully list the obstacles so God can clarify that the child will be his, rather than expressing doubt.
rows.anchor: ليس نصا في كون ذلك الغلام ولدا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation treats his question as praise of God's power, like marveling at a friend's generosity.
rows.anchor: ما ذكر ذلك للشك لكن على وجه التعظيم لقدرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation says his joy led him to verify the glad tidings, savor hearing them again, or emphasize the interpretation; Sarah's reaction to Isaac's announcement is a parallel.
rows.anchor: من شأن من بشر بما يتمناه أن يتولد له فرط السرور به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax of kadhālika can be nominative, meaning the matter is so before a new clause; accusative, pointing to an explanation that follows; or an assurance not to wonder, since the Lord's word has neither falsehood nor error.
rows.anchor: في قوله : { قال ربك هو هين } وجوه . أحدها : أن الكاف رفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further reading connects kadhālika to Zakariyyā's question: he asked whether God would make the couple young or grant a child while they remain old, and the answer says the child will come while they remain as they are.
rows.anchor: نهب الولد مع بقائك وبقاء زوجتك على الحاصلة في الحال

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads wa-huwa ʿalayya hayyin, which fits only the nominative interpretation: the matter is as stated, yet easy for God.
rows.anchor: قرأ الحسن وهو علي هين وهذا لا يخرج إلا على الوجه الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling an act easy for God is metaphorical, since difficulty cannot apply to Him; the meaning is that whatever He wills occurs.
rows.anchor: إطلاق لفظ الهين في حق الله تعالى مجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creating Zakariyyā from nothing demonstrates power to create bodies, qualities, and effects; creating a child from old parents requires only changing their qualities by restoring their reproductive capacity, as 21:90 says.
rows.anchor: لما خلقه من العدم الصرف والنفي المحض كان قادرا على خلق الذوات والصفات والآثار

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most interpreters say an angel speaks the phrase your Lord has said, while the promises around it are God's words.
rows.anchor: الجمهور على أن قوله قال كذلك قال ربك يقتضي أن القائل لذلك ملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī finds the angel interruption awkward between God's words and prefers God as speaker, as when a king reminds a servant that the ruler's promise obliges its fulfillment.
rows.anchor: والأولى أن يقال قائل هذا القول أيضا هو الله تعالى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say Zakariyyā asked for a sign to confirm the glad tidings; al-Rāzī calls this unlikely because God's explicit statement already confirms them.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم طلب الآية لتحقيق البشارة وهذا بعيد

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others say the announcement did not specify when the child would arrive, so he asked for a sign to learn the timing; al-Rāzī prefers this explanation.
rows.anchor: طلب الآية ليعرف بها وقت الوقوع وهذا هو الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sign is inability to speak; mere silence while able to speak would not be miraculous.
rows.anchor: اتفقوا على أن تلك الآية هي تعذر الكلام عليه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One view says Zakariyyā's tongue was entirely immobilized.
rows.anchor: أنه اعتقل لسانه أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī prefers that he could not converse with people but could remember God and read the Torah: total muteness might be illness and would need another sign to distinguish it, whereas selective inability proves divine action; the verse's mention of people implies he could speak to others.
rows.anchor: امتنع عليه الكلام مع القوم على وجه المخاطبة مع أنه كان متمكنا من ذكر الله

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take sawiyyan as describing the three nights.
rows.anchor: هو صفة لليالي الثلاث

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most interpreters take sawiyyan as describing Zakariyyā: he cannot speak to people although he remains well and has no illness.
rows.anchor: هو صفة لزكريا والمعنى : آيتك أن لا تكلم الناس في هذه المدة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One account says Zakariyyā had a private place for prayer and then went out to his people, gesturing to them.
rows.anchor: كان له موضع ينفرد فيه بالصلاة والعبادة ثم ينتقل إلى قومه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another account says people waited outside a shared prayer space for his permission; he came out unable to speak and signaled them.
rows.anchor: كان موضعا يصلي فيه هو وغيره إلا أنهم كانوا لا يدخلونه للصلاة إلا بإذنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awḥā cannot mean spoken words because speech was unavailable; he communicated by gesture, a sign, or writing, and the people understood that the promised event had occurred.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز أن يكون المراد من قوله أوحى إليهم الكلام لأن الكلام كان ممتنعا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gesture best fits the verse, since 3:41 describes the sign as communication only by symbol, which is not spoken language.
rows.anchor: الأشبه بالآية هو الإشارة لقوله تعالى في سورة آل عمران : { ثلاثة أيام إلا رمزا }

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators agree that tasbīḥ here means ritual prayer; Arabic can use the verb for prayer, as in ʿĀʾisha's phrase about performing the forenoon prayer.
rows.anchor: اتفق المفسرون على أنه أراد بالتسبيح الصلاة

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya says morning prayer means dawn prayer and evening prayer means afternoon prayer.
rows.anchor: روي عن أبي العالية أن البكرة صلاة الفجر والعشي صلاة العصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is possible the people customarily prayed these two prayers with him in the sanctuary, and he used to grant their entry verbally but signaled when his tongue was restrained.
rows.anchor: كانوا يصلون معه في محرابه هاتين الصلاتين فكان يخرج إليهم فيأذن لهم بلسانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's address to Yaḥyā shows that he had reached an age at which he could be addressed; the omitted explanation is understood from context.
rows.anchor: يدل على أن الله تعالى بلغ بيحيى المبلغ الذي يجوز أن يخاطبه بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book is likely the Torah, the scripture already familiar from the account of Israel, rather than a separate book specially given to Yaḥyā.
rows.anchor: ولا معهود ههنا إلا التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Take the book with strength means diligence and patience in carrying out prophetic duties, not mere physical ability to pick it up.
rows.anchor: ليس المراد منه القدرة على الأخذ لأن ذلك معلوم لكل أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation of ḥukm is wisdom, understanding the Torah, and insight into religion, supported by a line about a discerning girl judging doves.
rows.anchor: الأول : أنه الحكمة ومنه قول الشاعر : واحكم كحكم فتاة الحي

rows.speaker: معمر
rows.claim: Maʿmar interprets ḥukm as reason and reports that Yaḥyā said, We were not created to play.
rows.anchor: وهو قول معمر أنه العقل روي أنه قال ما للعب خلقنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī prefers that ḥukm means prophethood: the passage lists honors, prophethood is the greatest honor, and the word can mean authority to judge others.
rows.anchor: والأقرب حمله على النبوة لوجهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no special difficulty in a child having reason or prophethood unless one denies miracles; accepting extraordinary events removes the objection, since those are also departures from habit.
rows.anchor: فإنه ليس استبعاد صيرورة الصبي عاقلا أشد من استبعاد انشقاق القمر

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Ḥanān derives from yearning and distress at separation, like a camel's cry for its young; the Prophet's former palm trunk also moaned when he moved to the pulpit.
rows.anchor: أصله من الحنين وهو الارتياح والجزع للفراق

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some permit calling God al-Ḥannān in the sense of the compassionate and merciful.
rows.anchor: فأجازه بعضهم ، وجعله بمعنى الرؤوف الرحيم

rows.speaker: منهم
rows.claim: Others disallow the divine name because of the word's original associations and because no reliable report establishes it among God's names.
rows.anchor: لم يصح الخبر بهذه اللفظة في أسماء الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ḥanān describes God, one reading says He gave Yaḥyā judgment and mercy toward him, with zakāh as purification and honor.
rows.anchor: إنما آتيناه الحكم صبيا حنانا من لدنا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If divine ḥanān is for Zakariyyā, God says He answered his prayer by giving him a son and then granted that son judgment and mercy, purifying Zakariyyā from being a rejected supplicant.
rows.anchor: أن يكون الحنان من الله تعالى لزكريا عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If divine ḥanān is for Yaḥyā's community, God bestowed judgment and mercy on him for his people's benefit through his guidance.
rows.anchor: منا على أمته لعظيم انتفاعهم بهدايته وإرشاده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ḥanān describes Yaḥyā, it means tenderness toward people coupled with purity from neglecting obligations, since kindness can otherwise lead one to excuse wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: آتيناه التعطف على الخلق والطهارة عن المعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account also allows that Yaḥyā never sinned or even intended sin; Qur'anic commands to show gentleness and severity together illustrate why purity must constrain mercy.
rows.anchor: إنما جعلنا له التعطف على عباد الله مع الطهارة عن الإخلال بالواجبات

rows.speaker: عطاء بن رباح
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ ibn Rabāḥ interprets ḥanān as honor: Waraqa tells those torturing Bilāl that if they kill him he will honor him, as a parallel use.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية وجه آخر وهو المنقول عن عطاء بن رباح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة والضحاك وابن جريج
rows.claim: They interpret zakāh as a righteous, pure deed.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وقتادة والضحاك وابن جريج

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says Yaḥyā's zakāh made those who accepted him pure as well.
rows.anchor: زكاة لمن قبل منه حتى يكونوا أزكياء عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says God purified Yaḥyā by praise, as witnesses' testimony purifies a person.
rows.anchor: زكيناه بحسن الثناء كما تزكى الشهود الإنسان

rows.speaker: الكبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says Yaḥyā was a charitable gift that God bestowed on his parents.
rows.anchor: صدقة تصدق الله بها على أبويه عن الكبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakāh may also mean blessing and growth.
rows.anchor: خامسها : بركة ونماء وهو الذي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Yaḥyā's purity a gift from God supports the view that God creates human acts; explaining it as mere enabling grace departs from the apparent wording.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن هذا يدل على أن فعل العبد خلق لله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pious means both avoiding what God forbids and not neglecting what He commands; it is the highest praise and describes Yaḥyā, who neither sinned nor intended sin.
rows.anchor: يتقي نهي الله فيجتنبه ويتقي أمره فلا يهمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After worshiping God, honoring parents is the greatest act of devotion, as the command in 17:23 pairs service to parents with worship of God.
rows.anchor: لا عبادة بعد تعظيم الله تعالى مثل تعظيم الوالدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jabbār describes humility and gentleness, virtues of believers; humility before God makes arrogance toward others incoherent, while Iblīs's pride brought his exclusion.
rows.anchor: والمراد وصفه بالتواضع ولين الجانب وذلك من صفات المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another definition of jabbār is someone who recognizes no claim others may make on him because of his pride.
rows.anchor: الجبار هو الذي لا يرى لأحد على نفسه حقا

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyān says jabbār means quick to anger; wrongful punishment driven by personal anger is also called jabbār.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان في قوله : { جبارا عصيا } إنه الذي يقبل على الغضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAṣiyyan is more emphatic than ʿāṣī, just as ʿalīm is more emphatic than ʿālim.
rows.anchor: وهو أبلغ من العاصي كما أن العليم أبلغ من العالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The continuation of al-Ṭabarī's first view says God's peace protects Yaḥyā from grave punishment at death and punishment at resurrection.
rows.anchor: ويوم يموت } أي وأمان عليه من عذاب القبر : { ويوم يبعث حيا

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna says birth, death, and resurrection are the most isolating moments for people; God honored Yaḥyā with peace at all three.
rows.anchor: قال سفيان بن عيينة أوحش ما يكون الخلق في ثلاثة مواطن يوم يولد

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن نفطوية
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Naftawayh reads birth as the first sight of this world, death as the first sight of the afterlife, and resurrection as the first sight of Paradise and Hell; calling him alive points to martyrdom.
rows.anchor: وسلام عليه يوم ولد } أي أول ما يرى الدنيا { ويوم يموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The greeting may come from God or the angels, and its honor is the same because angels greet only by God's command.
rows.anchor: يمكن أن يكون من الله تعالى وأن يكون من الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaḥyā has a special distinction over other prophets because his greeting explicitly includes the day he was born, unlike the salutations to Noah and Abraham.
rows.anchor: ليحيى مزية في هذا السلام على ما لسائر الأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Jesus told Yaḥyā he was better because God greeted Yaḥyā while Jesus greeted himself.
rows.anchor: الثالث : روي أن عيسى عليه السلام قال ليحيى عليه السلام : أنت أفضل مني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says this comparison is unpersuasive: Jesus was infallible and spoke only by God's command, so his greeting himself is like God's greeting Yaḥyā.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس يقوى لأن سلام عيسى على نفسه يجري مجرى سلام الله على يحيى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Peace at birth must be a divine gift because Yaḥyā had done nothing to earn it; peace at death and resurrection could instead be reward.
rows.anchor: السلام عليه يوم ولد لا بد وأن يكون تفضلا من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first lesson in the story is etiquette in supplication: the quiet call shows that the best prayer is humble, concealed, and reliant on God's grace rather than one's own strength, as 7:55 teaches.
rows.anchor: وهو يدل على أن أفضل الدعاء ما هذا حاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raising the voice suggests strength and firmness, while lowering it conveys weakness and surrender, the proper posture of supplication.
rows.anchor: رفع الصوت مشعر بالقوة والجلادة وإخفاء الصوت مشعر بالضعف والانكسار
